articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities and Individuals for North Korea IT Worker Schemes and DRC-Related Activities
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) today announced new designations targeting individuals and entities involved in Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK) government-run information technology (IT) worker schemes. These schemes are designed to defraud U.S. businesses and generate revenue for the DPRK's illicit weapons of mass destruction (WMD) and ballistic missile programs.

Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent stated that the North Korean regime continues to exploit American companies through fraudulent activities conducted by its overseas IT operatives, who weaponize sensitive data and extort businesses for substantial payments. The Treasury aims to protect U.S. businesses from these malicious activities and hold those responsible accountable.

Additionally, OFAC announced Democratic Republic of the Congo-related designations, though specific details of these designations were not immediately available in the initial release. These actions underscore the U.S. government's commitment to countering illicit financial activities globally.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks, Inc. Reaches Settlement with OFAC Over Apparent Sanctions Violations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Extreme Networks, Inc. on October 27, 2026. This settlement addresses the company's potential civil liability for apparent violations of OFAC sanctions programs.

While the specific details of the violations were not immediately released in the OFAC announcement, such settlements typically involve companies that have engaged in transactions with sanctioned countries or individuals, or have failed to implement adequate sanctions compliance controls. These actions highlight OFAC's continued enforcement efforts to ensure adherence to U.S. sanctions regulations.
The settlement amount for Extreme Networks, Inc. was reported as $1,529,685, indicating the seriousness with which OFAC views these compliance failures.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends FAQs on Blocking, Rejecting Transactions, and Filing Reports
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued amended Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) regarding blocking and rejecting transactions and filing reports with OFAC. This update, released on October 26, 2026, is part of OFAC's ongoing process to review and ensure the currency of its published guidance.

The amendments cover several existing FAQs, including numbers 10, 32, 33, 34, 35, 36, 41, 42, 49, 50, and 53. These revisions aim to provide clearer guidance to U.S. persons and financial institutions on their obligations under OFAC regulations, particularly concerning the proper handling of blocked property and reporting requirements.
Such updates are crucial for compliance professionals to stay informed about the latest interpretations and expectations from OFAC, helping to mitigate the risk of sanctions violations.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Iran-Related and Russia-Related General Licenses, Amends FAQs, and Removes Belarus and North Korea Designations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced a series of actions, including new Iran-related and Russia-related General Licenses (GLs) and amended Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs).

Specifically, OFAC issued Iran General License GG, authorizing the wind down of transactions involving Karnakis and Karnakis, and Iran General License HH, authorizing wind-down activities, limited safety and environmental transactions, and the offloading of cargo involving certain blocked persons or vessels. Additionally, Russia-related General License 131K was issued, authorizing certain transactions for the negotiation of and entry into contingent contracts for the sale of Lukoil International GmbH and related maintenance activities.

In a significant development, OFAC also announced the removal of certain designations related to Belarus and North Korea from the Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List. This action included delisting Belarusian national Andrei Alekseevich Rybakov and Chinese national Lu Hezheng, along with two China-based animation studios. Furthermore, OFAC amended FAQs 1224 and 1225.

articles.headline: OFAC Implements PAIPA Designations and Issues Associated General Licenses
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA). These designations, made on October 19, 2026, target entities and individuals involved in activities that undermine American intellectual property.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC issued associated General Licenses (GLs) to provide guidance and authorization for certain related transactions. General License 1 authorizes transactions prohibited under PAIPA to the extent they are authorized or exempt under Cyber-related Sanctions Regulations.

General License 2 authorizes transactions ordinarily incident and necessary to the wind-down of any transaction involving certain entities designated on October 19, with a deadline of January 19, 2027. However, one designated entity, Zhisuan, is explicitly excluded from the scope of this authorization.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-Related General License and FAQ
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued an amended Venezuela-related General License (GL) and a Frequently Asked Question (FAQ). This update, released on October 16, 2026, aims to provide further clarity and adjust existing authorizations concerning transactions involving Venezuela.

These amendments are part of OFAC's ongoing efforts to fine-tune its sanctions programs in response to evolving political and economic conditions. The specific details of the changes to the General License and FAQ were not immediately available in the initial announcement but are crucial for entities engaging in authorized activities with Venezuela.
Such adjustments can impact various sectors, including humanitarian aid, certain commercial activities, and diplomatic engagements, reflecting a dynamic approach to sanctions implementation.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Iran-Related and Cuba Designations, Issues New and Amended General Licenses and FAQs
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new Iran-related designations and a Cuba designation on October 15, 2026. These actions target individuals and entities involved in activities deemed detrimental to U.S. national security and foreign policy interests.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC issued new and amended General Licenses (GLs) and Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs). These accompanying documents provide guidance on the scope of the new sanctions and outline authorized transactions or activities that might otherwise be prohibited.
The Iran-related designations are part of a broader effort to counter Iran's destabilizing activities, while the Cuba designation reinforces existing U.S. policy towards the island nation.

articles.headline: OFAC Removes Venezuela-Related Designation for Jorge Rodriguez
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced the removal of a Venezuela-related designation on October 14, 2026. This action specifically delists Jorge Rodriguez, the head of Venezuela's National Assembly.

Rodriguez, who has served as President of Venezuela's National Assembly since 2021, was initially designated in 2018. His delisting signals a significant shift in U.S. policy towards Venezuela, coming amid Washington's latest push for diplomacy and expansion of energy investment in the country.

The removal of sanctions on Rodriguez unblocks his assets subject to U.S. jurisdiction and lifts restrictive personal measures, potentially opening new channels for direct communication between Washington and Caracas.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations on October 13, 2026. These actions target individuals and entities involved in illicit drug trafficking and terrorist financing networks globally.

These designations aim to disrupt the financial infrastructure of criminal organizations and terrorist groups, preventing them from accessing the international financial system and undermining their ability to operate. The specific individuals and entities targeted were not detailed in the initial announcement but are now added to OFAC's Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List.
Such designations are a critical tool in the U.S. government's efforts to combat transnational crime and terrorism, reinforcing international security and stability.

articles.headline: Bank of America Settles with OFAC for $11.6 Million Over Sanctions Violations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced an $11,662,930 settlement with Bank of America, N.A. on October 13, 2026. This settlement resolves the bank's potential civil liability for 475 apparent violations of various OFAC sanctions programs, including those targeting Russia, Belarus, Iran, Burma, Somalia, narcotics, and global terrorism.

The apparent violations occurred due to Bank of America channeling correspondent banking payments through blocked banks, failing to prioritize alerts for exact name- and date of birth-matches to blocked persons, not promptly updating watchlists, and mishandling business accounts associated with blocked persons.

OFAC determined that the apparent violations were non-egregious but largely not voluntarily self-disclosed, leading to the substantial settlement amount. This action highlights the critical importance of robust sanctions compliance programs within financial institutions.

articles.headline: EU Adopts 22nd Sanctions Package Against Russia, Targeting Military-Industrial Complex
body: The European Union adopted its 22nd package of sanctions against Russia on October 12, 2026, in response to Russia's continued aggression against Ukraine. This package is primarily a listings package, adding 1,569 individuals and entities to the EU sanctions lists, including 826 Russian companies and 743 individuals.

The measures target companies forming part of the 'core' of Russia's military-industrial ecosystem, including businesses involved in the production and supply of components used in missiles, drones, military aircraft, and related defense technologies. The new designations bring the total number of listings under the Ukraine-related sanctions regime to almost 4,600.

The package also includes 77 political figures connected with the September 2026 elections in occupied Ukrainian territory, which the EU condemns as contrary to Ukrainian and international law. These measures were implemented through Council Decision (CFSP) 2026/2279 and Council Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/2281.
articles.source: Council of the European Union / Legal 500

articles.headline: EU Sanctions North Korean and Russian Targets for Supporting DPRK Weapons Programs
body: The Council of the European Union adopted additional restrictive measures against three individuals and four entities under its autonomous sanctions list on the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK) on October 12, 2026. These individuals and entities are deemed responsible for supporting, promoting, or facilitating activities that contribute to the DPRK's nuclear weapons, ballistic missiles, or other weapons of mass destruction programs, as well as for violating and evading United Nations sanctions.

The new listings specifically target activities linked to the growing military and economic cooperation between the DPRK and Russia, including the deployment of DPRK workers in Russia, commercial and industrial cooperation, and the 'arms-for-oil' trade, all in violation of UN Security Council prohibitions.

Among those listed is Ri Song Jin, a researcher at the DPRK National Aerospace Technology Administration and an official at the DPRK Missile General Bureau, who has been deployed to Russia as a technician supporting Russia's use of DPRK missiles. The Council also listed Russian real estate development company Samolet Group and its CEO, Anna Nikolaevna Akinshina.
articles.source: Council of the European Union / NK News

articles.headline: President Trump Waives New Russia Sanctions and Tariffs, Authorizes Russian Diesel Imports
body: President Donald Trump issued an executive order on October 16, 2026, waiving the majority of the Russia-related sanctions and tariffs introduced by the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026. This move effectively returns U.S. Russia-related sanctions to the status quo before the passage of the Act, though it does not affect the Iran-related sections.

The executive order also authorized the sale of Russian-origin diesel, a decision that has drawn bipartisan criticism from Congress. This action is seen as an effort to curb high gas prices in the U.S. and reflects a recurrent tension between the president and Congress regarding economic statecraft.

The Graham Act, signed into law on September 18, 2026, sought to codify existing executive order-based Russia sanctions, mandate new sanctions, and create new tariff authorities, including duties of up to 500% on goods from Russia and up to 100% on goods from top purchasers of Russian energy. However, these duties are currently waived.
articles.source: AP News / Clyde & Co / Snell & Wilmer

articles.headline: IRGC Intelligence Allegedly Orchestrates Takeover of Iran's Sanctioned Oil Trade
body: Documents and information obtained by Iran International suggest that the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Intelligence Organization has orchestrated a 'quasi-coup' to revive its corruption network and seize control of Iran's sanctioned oil trade.

This alleged takeover follows the dismissal of Oil Minister Mohsen Paknejad, which was reportedly planned for March but delayed due to the killing of Ali Khamenei and a subsequent 40-day conflict. A confidential letter from Khamenei's political adviser, Ali Shamkhani, reportedly requested the dismissal due to the oil minister's inability to manage a crisis involving trustees.

Sources familiar with the matter indicate that a primary reason for Shamkhani's discontent was the exclusion of Hossein Shamkhani, owner of a 51-vessel 'ghost fleet' used to circumvent sanctions, from sanctioned oil sales. This development suggests a significant internal power struggle over Iran's vital oil revenues amidst ongoing international sanctions.

articles.headline: Trump Administration Imposes Sweeping Sanctions on International Criminal Court
body: The Trump administration has imposed sweeping new sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) as part of its campaign to dismantle the tribunal. The U.S. believes the ICC has become politicized and has attempted to unfairly and illegally prosecute Americans and Israelis on war crimes charges.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced the sanctions, which long predated the Nobel Peace Prize being awarded to South African prosecutor Navi Pillay, a former judge at the ICC. This action underscores the Trump administration's strong opposition to the ICC's jurisdiction over U.S. personnel and allies.
The sanctions are expected to significantly impact the ICC's operations and personnel, further escalating tensions between the U.S. and the international judicial body.

articles.headline: OCC Announces October 2026 Enforcement Actions Against Banks and Individuals
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) released its enforcement actions for October 2026, detailing various penalties against banks and institution-affiliated parties (IAPs). These actions are taken to deter, encourage correction of, or prevent violations, unsafe or unsound practices, or breaches of fiduciary duty.

Among the actions against banks, American Express National Bank, Sandy, Utah, received a cease-and-desist order and a $350 million civil money penalty for deficiencies in its Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) compliance program, failure to timely file suspicious activity reports, and customer due diligence and customer identification program violations.

Additionally, Bank of America, National Association, Charlotte, North Carolina, was assessed a $750 million civil money penalty for similar BSA compliance program deficiencies, failure to timely file suspicious activity reports, and sending wires with inaccurate transmittor name information. The OCC also issued Orders of Prohibition against individuals, including Jennifer Hamblin, a Vault Teller at Fifth Third Bank, N.A., for embezzling customer funds, and Christopher Organista, a Former Operations Processor at U.S. Bank National Association, for embezzling bank customer funds.

body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) today announced a $750 million civil money penalty against Bank of America, N.A. (bank), for violations of the Bank Secrecy Act and its implementing regulations, including 12 CFR 21.21 and 12 CFR 21.11. This amount is the largest in OCC history.

articles.headline: Revisions to the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) revises the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing two addresses associated with Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. from the Entity List under the destination of China, People's Republic of (China). This determination follows the removal from the Entity List of Arrow China Electronics Trading Co., Ltd., and the removal of six aliases for Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. in November 2025.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
